title: Everyone studies Torah
hookLine: every Jew must study, rich or poor, healthy or sick, young or old
carry: no one is excused from torah study

lines: THE POOR? THE SICK? THE OLD?
cards: Who is excused? Surely the person too poor to spare an hour from finding bread. Surely the one who is sick.

Surely the old man whose strength is gone, or the father with a family to feed. Maimonides goes down the list, one by one, in his laws of Torah study, and his answer to each of them is the same. Not excused.

teach.h: RICH OR POOR, SICK OR WELL.
teach.b: Everyone studies. The law, in plain English: every man of Israel is obligated to study Torah, poor or rich, healthy or suffering, young or very old and weak. Even a poor man who lives on charity and goes door to door.
Even a man with a wife and children.
He must set a fixed time to study, by day and by night, because the verse says: "thou shalt meditate therein day and night." First, the list.
Maimonides names exactly the people anyone would excuse, and doesn't excuse them. Study is not a hobby for people with spare time.
Second, the fixed time. He doesn't ask for hours. He asks for a set time, kept.
A little, on purpose, regularly. Third, the examples. Among the great sages of Israel, he says, were woodcutters and water carriers, and some were blind, and still they studied day and night.
Until the day of death. Learning has no graduation. Now, honestly: Maimonides writes this as a duty of men.
A little later he says a woman who studies Torah receives reward, but he doesn't make it her obligation, and he adds cautions. Jewish communities read this differently today.
Some keep the obligation as he framed it, while also teaching women Torah seriously; others hold women and men to the same duty to learn.
Across those differences, the core still lands: being too busy, too poor or too old is not the end of learning.

how: Jewish tradition encourages fixed times for Torah study, alone, with a study partner, or in a class at synagogue, and some Jews follow a daily study cycle so that a little is learned every day.

o: a rule that only scholars may teach in public
a custom of studying Torah through one long night
the law that no one is too poor, sick or old to learn

p: a fixed time, by day and night

s: Maimonides excuses the poor and the sick from Torah study
he names them and says they are obligated too, with a fixed time to study.
some great sages, in his telling, worked as woodcutters and water carriers
and some were blind, and still they studied day and night.
he says a person may stop learning once they have learned enough
he says study continues until the day of death.

games.q: you're poor, you go door to door for bread, and you have a family to feed. does Maimonides say you must still study Torah?
o: no, survival comes first, so you are excused.
yes: set a fixed time to study, by day and by night.
games.why: he names exactly this case and says the obligation remains: set a time, because "thou shalt meditate therein day and night."

practice: Choose one short text you have nearby, a verse, a line from Pirkei Avot, a paragraph of anything that teaches, and read it once, slowly. Read it again, and notice one word you'd want to ask about.
Then close your eyes and turn that word over: a small, fixed time, kept.

wordCard.voice: Everyone studies. Maimonides' law that Torah study belongs to rich and poor, healthy and sick, young and old, with a fixed time, until the end of life. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the study of Torah, the name of Maimonides' laws on learning in the Book of Knowledge.

carryVoice: Your line: no one is excused from Torah study. A fixed time, kept, a little on purpose, for a whole life. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: thou shalt meditate therein day and night
